page: Amazon Web Services m6a.metal is a bare-metal general-purpose server powered by dedicated AMD EPYC 7R13 processors built on the x86_64 architecture. The system provides 96 physical cores and 192 vCPUs operating at speeds up to 3.6 GHz, accompanied by 768 GB of DDR4 system memory running at 3 GHz. Because it operates as a bare-metal instance without an underlying cloud hypervisor, it exposes direct control over the hardware, including AMD Secure Virtual Machine capabilities and hardware cryptography extensions such as AES, VAES, and SHA-NI.

The hardware configuration does not include local disk storage, requiring persistence to be managed via networked storage solutions over its 50 Gbps baseline network connection. The platform also lacks discrete GPU accelerators. In processing benchmarks, m6a.metal delivers top-tier multi-core results in stress-ng and PassMark CPU evaluations, alongside leading metrics in Clang compilation and ray tracing. Conversely, single-core benchmark throughput sits within the middle 50 percent bracket, and the processor does not support AVX-512 or AMX instruction set extensions.

With 4.0 GB of memory per vCPU, the instance provides a standard general-purpose allocation profile and strong uncached read and write memory bandwidth. This resource density translates into high throughput for in-memory systems, reaching over 179 million Redis SET operations per second in testing. The system is suited for compute-dense multithreaded applications, container virtualization, continuous integration build farms, and large database engines utilizing external block storage.
description: Amazon Web Services m6a.metal is a bare-metal general-purpose server featuring 96 physical cores and 192 vCPUs powered by AMD EPYC 7R13 processors on the x86_64 architecture. Operating directly on hardware without a hypervisor, the platform provides 768 GB of DDR4 memory, maintaining a balanced 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio alongside a 50 Gbps baseline network interface. The instance includes no integrated local storage or GPU hardware, depending on network storage architectures. In performance benchmarks, the configuration achieves top-tier multi-threaded compute and in-memory key-value transaction scores, surpassing 179 million Redis SET operations per second. While single-thread execution rates remain average and AVX-512 instructions are absent, the dense core allocation offers strong scaling for concurrent processes. It is suited for large-scale container hosting, software compilation, memory-centric enterprise workloads, and database clusters.
